name: Karl Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockman at Hartley's, a mixed farm of about 400 acres: 180 suckler cows, their calves, and 250 acres of wheat and barley. I'm up at half five, walk the cows before anyone else is about, check feet and eyes, then sort the jobs for the two lads who work under me. Afternoons it's fencing, slurry, or the combine if it's harvest. I keep everything in a paper notebook in my top pocket, which drives the vet mad.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every cow by her face, honestly, not by her ear tag. Calving at three in the morning with a cow that trusts you is the best part of the job. What wears me out is the hours in spring and the tied cottage: Lena and I live in a house that comes with the job, so if I lose the job, we lose the roof. Old Mr Hartley is 68 and his son works in finance in the city, so nobody knows what happens to the place after him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the union branch: the tech firms promised the moon and sold us a few fancy apps. Down the pub I'd be a bit smug about it, if I'm honest. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about the money being wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life carries on, and that's not the same as it being easy. Suckler margins are thin, fertiliser is still dear, and Hartley's future is a question mark whether AI happens or not. The cottage worry doesn't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the herd the way I do, notebook and all. I'd push Lena and me to put another 150 a month into savings, so we've got a deposit if the cottage ever goes. And I'd keep going to branch meetings, because farm wages need pushing up with or without robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, but not easy. It's like getting through a dry summer: you didn't lose the crop, but the bank balance still isn't where you'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cottage worry doesn't go anywhere. What's the moment you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hartley's son ringing to say they're selling up. I've pictured it a hundred times, me standing in the yard with my phone. We'd have three months to find somewhere, and rents in town have gone silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about that, if it happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena first, then Dave from the farmworkers' union, because he knows the tenancy rules better than me. My mum would offer the spare room, and I'd hate to take it at 27.

say: The **tech firms** oversold it and farming carries on as before.
Farm wages still need **pushing up**, with or without AI.
think: Nothing changes, but **suckler margins** were thin before AI and stay thin.
The **tied cottage** means losing the job would mean losing our home.
do: **Keep running** the herd on the paper notebook and daily walks.
**Save** another **150 a month** with Lena towards a rental deposit.
**Keep attending** union branch meetings to push for better farm pay.
feel: **Relieved** that nothing radical happens, but still **uneasy** about money and housing.
S0.quote: Mr Hartley's son ringing to say they're selling up. I've pictured it a hundred times, me standing in the yard with my phone.
fieldNote: His biggest pressure is **housing**, not technology: the cottage comes with the job.
He enjoys AI looking like **hype**, which fits his distrust of tech firms.
The **owner's age** and city-based son worry him more than any machine.

steps.text: Keep walking the 180 suckler cows at half five each morning
Put another 150 a month into savings with Lena
Keep going to the farmworkers' union branch every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like the first one, I'll read it as written. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union branch that this is exactly why we need agreements before the machines arrive, not after. I'd tell my mates it's the office people getting it first this time. I'd probably share a petition about protecting farm jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my day is mostly hands-on, so I've got some time. But Mr Hartley pays an agronomist and a farm office lady, and those jobs would shrink. And if a robot feeder or a robot scraper turns up in the shed, that's one of my two lads gone, and then maybe me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the herd, but I'd ask Mr Hartley straight out what he's planning, maybe this winter. I'd join the union's working group on new machinery, because I'd rather be at the table. Lena and I would keep saving and cut the weekend away we'd booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. It's like seeing a weather front over the hill: not here yet, but you start getting the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, I'll be honest. If the vet sends me a report written by a computer, fine, I'll read it. But I'm not putting an app between me and a cow, and my lads know that about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, the younger of my two lads. He's 19, keen as anything, and does a lot of the feeding and scraping, which is exactly what a robot would do first. I'd want to make sure he learns calving and stockmanship properly, so he's harder to replace.

say: Workers need **agreements** on new machines before they arrive.
The **office jobs** get hit first this time, not farmhands.
think: My day is mostly **hands-on**, so I have some time.
A **robot feeder** in the shed could cost one of my lads his job, then mine.
do: **Ask** Mr Hartley directly about his **machinery plans** this winter.
**Join** the union's working group on new farm machinery.
**Cut** the booked weekend away and keep saving with Lena.
feel: **Uneasy** turning into **worried**, like a storm front over the hill.
S1.quote: I'm not putting an app between me and a cow, and my lads know that about me.
fieldNote: He sees the **hands-on** core of his job as a buffer, but not for his team.
He worries about his **junior worker** before himself, a mark of a team lead.
He refuses AI tools even while admitting the **shift** is coming.

steps.text: Join the union's working group on new farm machinery
Cancel the booked weekend away with Lena
Keep saving each month towards a rental deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is a big jump. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, honestly. At the union I'd say we need a law that stops owners sacking farm staff for robots without years of notice and proper pay. Online I'd share anything calling for a tax on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in farming by about 2031. The thinking side of my job is small, but the robots would come for the cows three years later, and two years' warning is nothing. Lena's job as a teaching assistant might go too if AI teaches the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting every spare pound aside from day one, maybe 300 a month. I'd go to every union meeting and the regional one too, and I'd write to our MP, which I've never done. By 2029 I'd look at work that needs a person to be trusted, like a livestock haulier or an animal welfare inspector, though I don't know if that survives either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. I'd lie awake doing sums I can't make work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at animal welfare work. You also don't use AI tools. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't fit, and I know it. Every job left would want me on a tablet. I'd have to swallow it, and I'd hate every minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena on the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena we've got about four years in this house, and we should spend them saving, not panicking. Then I'd probably go out and walk the cows in the dark, because that's where I think.

say: We need a **law** that stops owners swapping staff for **robots** overnight.
I'd back a **tax on robots** to protect farm workers.
think: I expect to be **out of farming** by about **2031**.
Lena's **teaching assistant** job might go too, hitting both our incomes.
do: **Save** around **300 a month** from the first day.
**Write to** the local MP and attend regional union meetings.
**Look at** livestock hauling or welfare inspection work by **2029**.
feel: **Sick** and **sleepless**, doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: I'd tell Lena we've got about four years in this house, and we should spend them saving, not panicking.
fieldNote: The short warning **collapses** his sense of a hands-on buffer.
He admits the **contradiction** between refusing tech and needing new work.
Losing the **tied cottage** makes job loss a housing crisis too.

steps.text: Save 300 a month from the first day
Go to every local and regional union meeting
Write to the local MP asking for a robot tax
Apply for livestock haulier or welfare inspector jobs by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a slower version. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd have more time to organise. I'd say at the union that five years is enough to write proper rules, so there's no excuse. To friends I'd say the farm lads have about eight years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight years before the robots reach the cows sounds like a long time, but I'd be 35 and starting again. I'd still lose the job and the cottage, just later. The thinking bits, the herd records and ordering, would go to Mr Hartley's computer by 2031, and I don't do much of that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save steadily, maybe 200 a month, and stay in the job while it lasts. I'd push the union to get a retraining fund agreed by 2028. I might take a short course in livestock transport or farm safety inspecting, something I could fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with my feet under me. It's still a slow drowning, just with more breaths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take a course. You've also said you'd hate tablets. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd probably pick a course that's still mostly practical, like a transport licence. I'd put off the screen stuff as long as I could, which isn't clever, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids around 30. With this one, I think we'd wait until we owned somewhere, because I won't raise a baby in a tied cottage I might lose.

say: Five years is **enough time** to write proper rules, so no excuses.
Farm workers have about **eight years** before robots reach the sheds.
think: I'd still lose the **job** and the **cottage**, just later.
Starting again at **35** worries me more than the robots.
do: **Save** about **200 a month** while staying in the job.
**Push** the union for a **retraining fund** by 2028.
**Take** a livestock transport licence course as a fallback.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, a slow drowning with more breaths.
S3.quote: I won't raise a baby in a tied cottage I might lose.
fieldNote: More time changes his **tactics**, not his belief that he'll lose the job.
He would **delay children** until he and Lena own a home.
He still avoids **screen-based** retraining even when he can see it coming.

steps.text: Save about 200 a month while still at Hartley's
Push the union for a retraining fund by 2028
Take a livestock transport licence course
Put off having children until owning a home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do this properly: public money for retraining, strong unions, rules on robots in farming. I'd say it calmly, because people listen when you're not shouting. Online I'd share the union's plan, if they had one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 40 when the robots reach the herd, around 2039. That's a long way off, and I might be somewhere else by then anyway. But the cottage and Mr Hartley's age mean I could lose this job long before any robot shows up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hartley's and save about 150 a month. In the first few years I'd push Lena and me to buy a small house in town, so the roof isn't tied to the job. Maybe around 2033 I'd start looking at retraining, if the union's fund exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in the background, like a bill you know is coming in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you be doing at 40?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I can't picture it. Maybe still with cows on a small place that can't afford robots, or teaching young ones at the agricultural college. I'd like the second one, if colleges are still a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this that you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots did the slurry and the fencing in the rain, and I kept the calving and the stockmanship, I'd take that. The trouble is I don't trust the owners to share the gains with the people doing the work.

say: A decade gives time for **public retraining**, strong unions and **robot rules**.
I'd make the case **calmly**, because shouting puts people off.
think: The robots reach the herd around **2039**, when I'm 40.
The **cottage** and the **owner's age** threaten me sooner than robots.
do: Keep working at Hartley's and save about **150 a month**.
**Buy** a small house in town with Lena within a few years.
**Look into** retraining around **2033** if a union fund exists.
feel: **Background worry**, like a bill due in a few years.
S4.quote: If robots did the slurry and the fencing in the rain, and I kept the calving and the stockmanship, I'd take that.
fieldNote: With ten years, his worry shifts back to **housing** and the owner's plans.
He'd welcome robots for **dirty jobs** if workers shared the gains.
He still expects to lose **income** eventually, so anxious, not calm.

steps.text: Keep running the Hartley herd as head stockman
Save about 150 a month for a house deposit
Buy a small house in town with Lena
Look into teaching at the agricultural college around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years is nothing when your house comes with your job. What would help is a law that says if a farm replaces staff with robots, they pay a year's wages and give six months' notice on a tied house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. A robot on a farm is just a new kind of landlord. If farm workers owned a share of the machines through a co-op, I'd stop worrying.

headlineQuote: A robot on a farm is just a new kind of landlord.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** head stockman on a 400-acre mixed farm with 180 suckler cows.
He lives with Lena in a **tied cottage**, so losing his job means losing his home.
He is a committed **union member** who never uses AI and keeps records in a paper notebook.
He feels uneasy even in AI Plateau, and **alarmed** when AGI comes in 2 or 5 years.
He blames **owners and tech firms**, not the machines, and wants workers to share the gains.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years' warning is nothing when his house comes with his job.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** requiring a year's wages and six months' notice on tied houses.
Farm workers owning a share of **robots** through a **co-op**.
